Learning to Read

From being read to, to the first own book: this story encourages your child to keep reading on their own.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

Every evening the same familiar ritual: your child snuggles in, and you read aloud. But now they're suddenly supposed to read themselves — and pushes the book straight back to you: "You read, it takes too long for me." A single sentence costs visible effort, the book ends up unread under the bed, and you wonder how the child who loves stories suddenly became a child who avoids books.

Between ages 6 and 9, decoding individual words is still slow and effortful — the brain has to piece together letter by letter what arrived effortlessly as a flow when read aloud. This gap between the inner expectation ("I want to understand the story") and the actual pace frustrates many children. Whoever gets the early feeling of "I'm bad at reading" starts avoiding books — and that very avoidance then slows down the practice needed to get better.

Because a book character isn't your child's own sibling or the classmate at the next desk, watching them struggle with reading feels less exposing. Your child recognizes their own hesitation in the character and senses: other kids wrestle with single words too. The small progress the character makes by the end becomes a quiet promise for their own reading — already rehearsed mentally before their own book is opened again.

In the personalized story, your child — with their own face on every page — sits in the familiar reading nook at home and finds, page by page, their own way from being read to toward reading independently. The story is deliberately kept simple in language and sentence length, so that reading itself becomes the first small success. The first story is free to try — maybe the first book your child finishes entirely on their own.

Keep the shared read-aloud time even once your child reads on their own — it doesn't have to be either-or. Let your child choose books themselves, even thin or "too easy" ones; every page read counts. Celebrate small progress concretely rather than with general praise. If letters remain regularly reversed or decoding stays unusually effortful beyond second or third grade, it's worth having reading difficulties assessed by the school or a specialist.

What your child learns

Independent reading, perseverance, vocabulary, enjoyment of reading, self-confidence.

Recommended age

6-9 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I motivate my child to read on their own?

Let your child choose what they read themselves, even if it's very short or "too easy" — the freedom to choose makes reading their own thing rather than a chore. Praising small wins concretely ("you got through the whole page by yourself") works better than general praise.

Is it a problem if my child doesn't want to give up being read to?

Not at all. Being read to and reading independently don't cancel each other out — many children benefit from still being read to while reading shorter texts on their own in parallel. The shared ritual stays important for the enjoyment of stories.

How do I know if my child has dyslexia?

Signs can include persistently reversed letters, unusually slow decoding despite practice, or strong frustration with reading that goes beyond the usual level. A reliable assessment comes from the teacher or a dyslexia specialist, not from a single sign noticed at home.

Which books are suitable for a child's first attempts at reading alone?

Short sentences, plenty of pictures, a familiar topic, and a font size that doesn't tire the eyes help the most. More important than the "right" difficulty level is often that the child chose the book themselves.

My child compares themselves to classmates who read better — what should I do?

Explain that every child learns to read at their own pace and that comparisons rarely help. Direct attention to your own child's progress from last week to today, rather than to other children in the class.
